source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, sides field says mirrored/same; price-level conditions rejected (shift test); primitives (failure-test trigger, measured-move target, trend-line/channel failure entry, support bounce entry, spring/upthrust, climax bar) are redefined fresh in this file per the mining brief even though Chapter 5 defines equivalents -- the dedup pass merges across files

candidates.name: FailureTestOfLevelTrigger
candidates.quote: For a short entry, the market trades above a clearly defined resistance area, but immediately reverses on the same or the following bar and closes back under the resistance. ... Enter short on the close of the bar that closes back below resistance.
candidates.description: Primitive: price trades beyond a significant level, then within maxBarsBeyond bars closes back on the origin side of that level. Enter on the close of the bar that closes back across the level.
candidates.pseudocode: barsBeyondLevel <= maxBarsBeyond AND close[0] crosses back to the origin side of level (where barsBeyondLevel counts consecutive bars with a high/low beyond level since it was first breached)
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close of the reversal bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: cross-bar persistent counter since the level was breached

notes: The book's default is 'same or the following bar' (maxBarsBeyond = 1), tighter than Chapter 5's rule-of-thumb 'two or three bars'.

candidates.name: MeasuredMoveObjectiveTarget
candidates.quote: the measured move objective (MMO), which is calculated by taking the length of the setup leg (AB in Figure 6.8), adding that number to the pivot point marked C, and expecting the CD leg to be approximately the same length as the AB leg.
candidates.description: Primitive profit target: project the length of a prior (setup) swing leg forward from a later pivot point, expecting the next leg to be of similar length. Reused as a target by several templates in this file.
candidates.pseudocode: target = pivotCPrice + (legAB_HighPrice - legAB_LowPrice)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (profit target, limit at target level)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to identify leg AB and pivot C

notes: Grimes treats this as a zone, not an exact level: 'consider it a zone... take partial or complete profits even though the trade had not quite reached the target.'

candidates.name: TrendLineChannelFailureReversalEntry
candidates.quote: The entry trigger is a failure of this trend line or channel, followed by an immediate reversal; that is, the line is penetrated, but prices recover back above the trend line within a few bars.
candidates.description: Primitive pullback trigger 1: a trend line or channel line bounding the pullback is penetrated, then price recovers back across it within a few bars. Approximated without true trend-line projection as a break-and-recover of the pullback's own recent low/high (a channel-line proxy).
candidates.pseudocode: low[1] < lowest(low[2], pullbackLookback) AND close[0] > lowest(low[2], pullbackLookback)
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close back above the line -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: the book's actual trigger needs a drawn trend line or parallel channel from pivots; this is a lowest-low proxy in place of the line

candidates.name: SupportResistanceBounceEntry
candidates.quote: The second entry trigger is actually buying against the support at the bottom of the pullback.
candidates.description: Primitive pullback trigger 2: buy (sell) directly against the support (resistance) level defined by the pullback's own recent low (high), on a limit basis.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] <= lowest(low[1], pullbackLookback) + touchTolerance * atr(atrLookback)
candidates.book_order_type: limit entry at the support/resistance level -> mechanized as close-and-next-open once the bar touches the level

complexity.reason: window low/high plus an ATR-scaled touch tolerance

notes: Stop placement is problematic for this trigger per the book, because support can break before recovering -- see G06-17.

candidates.name: SpringUpthrustAtRangeExtreme
candidates.quote: wait for springs (i.e., drops below the support at the bottom of the base that immediately recover back above the support level) and enter on the close of those bars.
candidates.description: Primitive: a spring at range support -- the bar's low trades below the recent range low but closes back above it. Mirrored as an upthrust at resistance for shorts.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < lowest(low[1], rangeLookback) AND close[0] > lowest(low[1], rangeLookback)
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close of the spring/upthrust bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: window low plus a close comparison

candidates.name: ClimaxBarCondition
candidates.quote: It is usually a good idea to avoid pullbacks after conditions that could indicate a buying or selling climax. We have looked at these parabolic expansions and have seen that they frequently cap trends.
candidates.description: Primitive: a bar (or the most recent bar) shows range/momentum expansion well beyond normal -- a buying or selling climax.
candidates.pseudocode: (high[0] - low[0]) > climaxMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback])

complexity.reason: single bar's range vs. a window average

candidates.name: MomentumDivergenceMatureTrendSetup
candidates.quote: The best examples of this trade occur in mature, extended trends, and will usually be accompanied by momentum divergence on the trading time frame.
candidates.description: Failure Test setup condition 1: momentum fails to make a new extreme alongside a new price extreme in a mature, extended trend.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] >= highest(high[1], lookback) AND momentumValue[0] < momentumValueAtPriorExtreme

complexity.reason: cross-bar comparison of momentum at two price-extreme bars

candidates.name: ConsolidationBelowResistanceSetup
candidates.quote: Another common variation occurs in an extended consolidation just under resistance. This type of consolidation would normally have a high expectation of producing another trend leg above that resistance, so many traders are monitoring the area.
candidates.description: Failure Test setup condition 2: a tight recent range sits just under (over) a longer-window's resistance (support) extreme -- primes a failure test if the eventual breakout fails.
candidates.pseudocode: tightHigh = highest(high, tightLookback); tightLow = lowest(low, tightLookback); rangeHigh = highest(high, rangeLookback); (tightHigh - tightLow) < tightFraction * (rangeHigh - lowest(low, rangeLookback)) AND (rangeHigh - tightHigh) < proximityFraction * (rangeHigh - lowest(low, rangeLookback))

complexity.reason: two window highest/lowest comparisons, no pivots

notes: Same mechanics as the Chapter 5 'tight range near the edge of a larger range' primitive, redefined here as a Failure Test precondition.

candidates.name: FailureTestStopBeyondExcursionExtreme
candidates.quote: The stop for this trade is clearly defined: a hard stop must be entered just beyond the extreme of the test beyond the level.
candidates.description: Stop placed just beyond the highest high (short) / lowest low (long) reached during the excursion beyond the level, including the bar before entry if that bar set the extreme.
candidates.pseudocode: stopPrice = highest(high, barsBeyondLevel + 1) + stopBuffer * ctx.MinMove()
candidates.book_order_type: hard stop -> close-and-next-open if breached, or intrabar stop order

complexity.reason: needs the excursion's own high-water mark tracked across the setup bars

candidates.name: FailureTestFirstTargetAtInitialRisk
candidates.quote: one plan would be to take profit on the first part when the profit equals the initial risk on the trade.
candidates.description: Take (partial) profit once open profit reaches the initial per-share/point risk (entry price to stop price) of the trade.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= abs(ctx.EntryPrice() - initialStopPrice) * riskMultiple

complexity.reason: needs the initial stop distance carried as position state

candidates.name: FailureTestStallWarningExit
candidates.quote: if you enter short on B in Figure 6.1 and the market spends two to three days trading above 105, this is most likely a precursor of a losing trade. Reduce exposure or close out these trades if they do not work quickly in your favor.
candidates.description: If the position has been held for stallBars bars without reaching the first profit target and price has consolidated near the entry level (small range since entry), exit or reduce exposure.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.BarsSinceEntry() >= stallBars AND ctx.OpenPositionProfit() < riskMultiple * abs(ctx.EntryPrice() - initialStopPrice) AND (highest(high, stallBars) - lowest(low, stallBars)) < stallFraction * abs(ctx.EntryPrice() - initialStopPrice)

complexity.reason: cross-bar state on bars-since-entry plus a range-contraction test

candidates.name: FailureTestReentryAfterStopOut
candidates.quote: some of these trades will hit the stop point and, on the same or the next bar following the stop-out bar, will once again fall back inside the level. ... this second trade, taken on the second failure, is also an excellent entry.
candidates.description: If a Failure Test trade was stopped out (price made a new extreme beyond the excursion), and on the same or the following bar price closes back inside the level again, take a second failure-test entry in the same direction as the first.
candidates.pseudocode: priorFailureTestStoppedOut[reentryLag] == true AND close[0] crosses back to the origin side of level
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close back inside the level -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: needs the prior stop-out tracked as recent trade-history state

notes: This is the mirror image of LastTradeCooldown's usual purpose: here a recent loss on the SAME setup is a reason to re-enter, not to stand down.

candidates.name: FailureTestTemplate
candidates.quote: The failure test pattern is the classic Wyckoff spring and upthrust; the only adaptation is the addition of a firm stop level and a concrete trading plan.
candidates.description: The book's named Failure Test template in full: setup (mature-trend momentum divergence, G06-07, OR consolidation under resistance, G06-08) + trigger (G06-01) + stop (G06-09) + first target (G06-10) + stall-warning management (G06-11) + reentry-on-second-failure (G06-12).
candidates.pseudocode: (G06-07 OR G06-08) AND G06-01, managed by G06-09/G06-10/G06-11, with G06-12 as a standing reentry rule
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close of the reversal bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: aggregates several moderate primitives; no swing-pivot detection required

notes: Also known as Victor Sperandeo's '2B' trade (page 169).

candidates.name: SetupLegAtLeastAsStrongAsPriorLegs
candidates.quote: if the market is in an established trend, the preceding setup leg should be at least as strong as previous trend legs in the same direction. In other words, it should not break the pattern of the trend and should not show momentum divergence.
candidates.description: Pullback setup: the trend leg immediately preceding the pullback is at least as large (price extent) as the average of the preceding same-direction legs.
candidates.pseudocode: setupLegLength >= average(priorSameDirectionLegLengths, numPriorLegs)

complexity.reason: needs swing-leg detection and length comparison across several legs

candidates.name: PullbackReducedRangeActivity
candidates.quote: Good pullbacks almost always show reduced activity (smaller ranges for individual bars) and the absence of strong countertrend momentum.
candidates.description: The average bar range during the pullback is smaller than the average bar range of the preceding setup leg.
candidates.pseudocode: average(high[0..pullbackBars-1] - low[0..pullbackBars-1]) < reducedFraction * average(high[pullbackBars..pullbackBars+legBars-1] - low[pullbackBars..pullbackBars+legBars-1])

complexity.reason: two window range averages

candidates.name: AvoidThreeOrMoreSupportTestsInPullback
candidates.quote: One pattern to avoid is buying against multiple (three or more) tests of support in a pullback, as this pattern is often more indicative of an impending failure. The operative concept here is usually lower highs into support.
candidates.description: Do not take the pullback support-bounce trigger (G06-04) if the pullback has already tested its own support/resistance level maxTests or more times, with each bounce's high (low) lower (higher) than the previous.
candidates.pseudocode: testCount(low[i] near pullbackSupport, i = 0..pullbackBars) >= maxTests AND bounceHigh[0] < bounceHigh[1]

complexity.reason: needs a touch counter plus lower-highs (higher-lows) comparison across bounces

candidates.name: PullbackStopBeyondPatternWithBuffer
candidates.quote: My preference is to put stops farther away from the pattern... If you put yours a few ticks or cents beyond the obvious levels, you may still be swept out if there is extra volatility beyond the level.
candidates.description: Stop placed beyond the pullback's own extreme, offset by a small ATR-scaled buffer past the obvious level (rather than exactly at the pattern edge).
candidates.pseudocode: stopPrice = lowest(low, pullbackLookback) - bufferAtrMultiple * atr(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: window low/high plus an ATR-scaled buffer

notes: Grimes's stated 'small random jitter' component is rejected separately (randomness); the deterministic buffer captures the rest of the idea.

candidates.name: PullbackConservativeTargetPriorSwing
candidates.quote: The most conservative profit target is at the previous pivot high of the setup leg for long traders, or at the low of the setup leg for shorts.
candidates.description: Take profit at the pivot high (long) / low (short) that started the pullback -- the previous swing extreme.
candidates.pseudocode: target = highest(high, ctx.BarsSinceEntry() + priorLegLookback)

complexity.reason: window highest/lowest

candidates.name: PullbackRiskMultipleTarget
candidates.quote: it also makes sense to incorporate information from the conservative and MMO profit targets... taking partial profits at one or two times (1x or 2x) the initial risk on the trade.
candidates.description: Take (partial) profit at a multiple of the initial risk (entry-to-stop distance) on the trade.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= riskMultiple * abs(ctx.EntryPrice() - initialStopPrice)

complexity.reason: needs the initial stop distance carried as position state

candidates.name: ScratchExitOnTrendIntegrityLoss
candidates.quote: A pullback may emerge at a spot where the trade was justified, but developing price action may suggest that the trend is losing integrity. If this happens... it is often advisable to scratch the trade, exiting for a small win or loss.
candidates.description: If within a few bars of entry a strong bar forms against the trade direction (proxy for 'the trend is losing integrity'), scratch the trade at market rather than holding to the original stop.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.BarsSinceEntry() <= scratchWindow AND (opposite-direction bar body) > bodyMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback])

complexity.reason: 'losing integrity' is a qualitative read; mechanized here as an early strong opposite-direction bar

candidates.name: PullbackTemplate
candidates.quote: Pullbacks are probably the most important structural feature of trends... using the countertrend pullback to position in the larger trend at an advantageous price.
candidates.description: The book's named Pullback (Buying Support or Shorting Resistance) template in full: setup (strong setup leg G06-14, reduced pullback activity G06-15, avoid 3+ support tests G06-16) + trigger (trend-line failure reversal G06-03 OR support bounce G06-04) + stop (G06-17) + targets (conservative prior swing G06-18, risk-multiple G06-19, MMO G06-02) + management (scratch on integrity loss G06-20).
candidates.book_order_type: mixed: G06-03 is stop/market on the close-back bar, G06-04 is a limit entry

complexity.reason: aggregates hard leg-comparison setup conditions with the trend-line-proxy trigger

notes: Trade type: trend continuation. Encompasses flags, pennants, wedges, and continuation triangles per the book -- Grimes treats them as functionally identical, so no separate candidates were made for each named shape.

candidates.name: LowerTimeFrameBreakoutEntryApprox
candidates.quote: This trade setup times the entry into the pullback by using the momentum of a lower time frame breakout so that the trade will be entered when the market is moving in the intended direction of the trade.
candidates.description: Enter the pullback on a breakout of a short-lookback high/low, approximating a lower-time-frame breakout with a much shorter window on the same (trading-time-frame) bars.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] > highest(high[1], ltfLookback)
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry on the lower-time-frame breakout -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: a short Highest/Lowest window standing in for a genuinely lower time frame

notes: Higher/lower-time-frame reasoning approximated per the mining brief: a 3-bar breakout on the trading time frame stands in for a breakout on a several-times-faster chart. No exact ratio given by the book.

candidates.name: EqualHighsBreakoutWithinPullback
candidates.quote: if a series of two to three bars all have the same high, paying a breakout through those highs is often a good entry.
candidates.description: Two to three consecutive bars within the pullback share (approximately) the same high; enter on a breakout above that shared high.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(high[1] - high[2]) < tickTolerance * ctx.MinMove() AND close[0] > highest(high[1], equalBarsCount)
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry on the breakout of the equal highs -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: small-window equality test plus a breakout comparison

candidates.name: TightStopBeyondLtfTriggerBar
candidates.quote: many traders will want to use a very tight stop, operating under the assumption that if the breakout is truly a critical tipping point, they can simply exit the market for a very small loss.
candidates.description: The tight-stop school for the lower-time-frame breakout trigger: stop just beyond the low (high) of the breakout trigger bar itself.
candidates.pseudocode: stopPrice = low[triggerBarLag] - stopBuffer * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: a bare comparison to a single bar's extreme

notes: Grimes explicitly prefers G06-25 over this approach (see its notes).

candidates.name: WiderStopTrueToPatternGeometry
candidates.quote: My preference is to use a larger stop that is true to the geometry of the trading time frame pattern.
candidates.description: Grimes's preferred stop for the lower-time-frame breakout entry: the standard pullback stop (G06-17), sized to the trading-time-frame pattern rather than the tight lower-time-frame trigger bar.
candidates.pseudocode: same as G06-17: stopPrice = lowest(low, pullbackLookback) - bufferAtrMultiple * atr(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: same as G06-17

candidates.name: PullbackLtfBreakoutTemplate
candidates.quote: This trade setup addresses the key issue of precisely timing the entry into the pullback pattern.
candidates.description: The book's named Pullback, Entering Lower Time Frame Breakout template: same pullback setup as G06-21 (G06-14, G06-15) + trigger on a lower-time-frame breakout (G06-22 OR the equal-highs variant G06-23) + stop (tight G06-24 OR the preferred wider G06-25) + standard pullback targets (G06-18, G06-19, G06-02).
candidates.pseudocode: G06-14 AND G06-15 AND (G06-22 OR G06-23), managed by G06-25 (preferred) or G06-24, with G06-18/G06-19/G06-02 as targets
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry on the lower-time-frame breakout -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: inherits the hard pullback setup plus the LTF-approximation trigger

notes: Trade type: trend continuation and breakout blend. Better momentum confirmation, worse trade location and larger stops than the plain Pullback template.

candidates.name: ComplexPullbackAbcdTwoLegs
candidates.quote: A complex pullback is a complete ABCD trend structure itself: the first countertrend leg is a lower time frame trend... followed by a retracement... which is then followed by another countertrend leg.
candidates.description: The pullback contains two distinct countertrend legs separated by a with-trend retracement (an ABCD structure) rather than one simple leg.
candidates.pseudocode: swingLow[0] (D) exists after a with-trend retracement swingHigh[1] (C) that followed an earlier countertrend swingLow[2] (B) off swingHigh[3] (A), all within the pullback window

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and leg sequencing

candidates.name: HiddenComplexPullbackCandleColorCue
candidates.quote: This second complex pullback pattern is one or two with-trend candles in the middle of what otherwise looks like a simple pullback.
candidates.description: One or two bars with a body colored in the trend direction (close beyond open in the trend's direction) appear in the middle of an otherwise simple, against-trend-colored pullback -- a cue that the pullback is complex even though it looks simple on the trading time frame.
candidates.pseudocode: count(i = midStart..midEnd, sign(close[i] - open[i]) == trendDirection) between 1 and 2, while the bars flanking that window are colored against the trend

complexity.reason: a bar-body-direction sequence test over a small fixed window

candidates.name: AvoidSimplePullbackAfterClimax
candidates.quote: It is usually a good idea to avoid pullbacks after conditions that could indicate a buying or selling climax.
candidates.description: Block the simple Pullback template (G06-21) if a climax bar (G06-06) occurred within the recent lookback; a with-trend trade is still possible, but only via the complex-pullback template (G06-32), not the simple one.
candidates.pseudocode: NOT (any of the last climaxLookback bars satisfies ClimaxBarCondition)

complexity.reason: a short OR-window over the climax primitive

candidates.name: ComplexPullbackLegEqualityTarget
candidates.quote: both countertrend legs of the pullback tend to be similar lengths, so it is often possible to predict the general area where the second leg will stop using a measured move objective (AB = CD).
candidates.description: In a complex pullback, project the second countertrend leg (CD) to be approximately the same length as the first (AB) -- the same MMO mechanics as G06-02, specialized to the two legs of this pattern.
candidates.pseudocode: target = pivotCPrice - (legAB_HighPrice - legAB_LowPrice) (mirrored sign for shorts)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (limit profit target / expected reversal zone)

complexity.reason: needs the same swing-pivot detection as G06-27

candidates.name: StopBeyondSecondLegExtreme
candidates.quote: in complex pullbacks this is often an excellent risk point... the stop level is more clearly defined.
candidates.description: Stop placed just beyond the extreme (termination point) of the second (CD) countertrend leg of a complex pullback.
candidates.pseudocode: stopPrice = legCD_LowPrice - stopBuffer * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: needs the second leg's own swing extreme, from G06-27's pivot detection

candidates.name: ComplexPullbackTemplate
candidates.quote: Complex pullbacks, which are pullbacks composed of two distinct countertrend legs, are very common, especially in mature trends.
candidates.description: The book's named Trading Complex Pullbacks template: setup (two-leg ABCD structure G06-27, or the hidden candle-color cue G06-28; may follow a climax where the simple template G06-21 is blocked by G06-29) + trigger (support bounce G06-04 or trend-line failure reversal G06-03, same as the simple pullback) + stop (G06-31, clearer than the simple pullback's) + target (leg-equality MMO, G06-30).
candidates.book_order_type: mixed: G06-03 is stop/market on the close-back bar, G06-04 is a limit entry

complexity.reason: requires swing-pivot detection for the ABCD structure

notes: Trade type: trend continuation. The book flags a real risk-management question -- taking this trade shortly after a loss on the simple pullback that preceded it -- but that reduces to position sizing and is not mechanized (see rejected).

candidates.name: TrendTerminationPreconditionPattern
candidates.quote: The first is that the market must have made a pattern that suggests the current trend could be terminating... loss of momentum on successive thrusts, an extremely overextended market on the higher time frame, some type of double top or bottom formation... or perhaps a failure test.
candidates.description: The Anti's first setup condition: some prior pattern suggesting the trend could be ending -- momentum divergence across successive thrusts (reuses G06-07's mechanics), high volatility/overextension (reuses G06-06's climax mechanics), or a completed failure test (G06-01).
candidates.pseudocode: MomentumDivergenceAcrossThrusts OR ClimaxBarCondition (recent) OR FailureTestOfLevelTrigger (recent, against the established trend)

complexity.reason: an OR of several sub-conditions, one of which (double top/bottom) needs pattern recognition over a variable-length window and is only approximated by the others here

notes: The 'double top or bottom formation' sub-case is not separately mechanized; it reduces to two roughly-equal swing highs/lows, which is closer to a design decision than a bar-level test.

candidates.name: CountertrendSpikeStrongerThanPriorSwings
candidates.quote: the market then makes a move that shows a distinct change of character, such as a shift of momentum against the old trend. In the case of an uptrend, a downswing would emerge that was much stronger than previous downswings.
candidates.description: The Anti's second setup condition: a countertrend swing emerges that is larger (in price) than the average of the recent countertrend swings in the established trend -- a change of character.
candidates.pseudocode: abs(currentCountertrendSwingLength) > characterMultiple * average(priorCountertrendSwingLengths, numPriorSwings)

complexity.reason: needs swing-leg detection and comparison against prior countertrend swings

candidates.name: AntiFirstPullbackTrigger
candidates.quote: The actual entry for this trade is in the first pullback following the strong countertrend price movement.
candidates.description: After G06-33 and G06-34 both fire, enter on the first pullback following the countertrend spike, using either standard pullback trigger (trend-line failure reversal G06-03, or support/resistance bounce G06-04).
candidates.pseudocode: G06-33 AND G06-34 fired recently AND (G06-03 OR G06-04) on the first pullback since the spike
candidates.book_order_type: mixed: G06-03 is stop/market on the close-back bar, G06-04 is a limit entry

complexity.reason: combines two hard setup conditions with a pullback trigger

candidates.name: AntiLooseEntryAnywhereInPullback
candidates.quote: Because this is a countertrend trade, your risk point is clearly defined so you can simply enter anywhere into that first pullback with a stop outside the existing trend extreme.
candidates.description: The Anti's third, loosest trigger: once the setup (G06-33, G06-34) has fired, enter at the next bar's open during the first pullback, without waiting for a specific trigger bar, using a stop beyond the trend extreme.
candidates.pseudocode: G06-33 AND G06-34 fired recently AND ctx.MarketPosition() == 0 -> enter at next open
candidates.book_order_type: market entry at the next bar's open

complexity.reason: a direct entry once the setup condition is true, no additional trigger bar test

notes: The book calls this 'not ideal in most cases.'

candidates.name: AntiStopBeyondTrendExtreme
candidates.quote: One choice is to simply put the stop beyond the trend extreme... If the level is violated, we know the countertrend attempt has failed and the probabilities favor trend continuation.
candidates.description: Conservative Anti stop: placed beyond the pre-Anti trend's own extreme pivot (the highest high / lowest low of the established trend leading into the spike).
candidates.pseudocode: stopPrice = highest(high, trendLookback) + stopBuffer * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: window highest/lowest over the trend's own lookback

candidates.name: AntiMmoFirstTarget
candidates.quote: It is very common to see the first thrust after the initial pullback exhaust itself at the MMO, and then to see the market turn back down and eventually violate the previous trend extreme.
candidates.description: Apply the measured-move-objective target (G06-02) to the Anti's first thrust out of the pullback: the length of the countertrend spike projected forward from the pullback's end.
candidates.pseudocode: target = pullbackEndPrice - (spikeHighPrice - spikeLowPrice) (mirrored sign for shorts)
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (limit profit target / management inflection zone)

complexity.reason: same swing/leg-length requirement as G06-02

candidates.name: AntiProtectProfitsIfMmoHolds
candidates.quote: If, however, it holds and there is no continued countertrend momentum (and the pattern suggests a complex consolidation), be very protective of any remaining profits in the position.
candidates.description: If price reaches the MMO zone (G06-38) but fails to break through it (no new countertrend extreme within a few bars), tighten the stop to breakeven or better on the remaining position.
candidates.pseudocode: priceReachedMmoZone == true AND ctx.BarsSinceEntry() - mmoReachedBar > confirmBars AND close[0] has not exceeded the MMO zone -> tighten stop to ctx.EntryPrice()

complexity.reason: cross-bar state tracking whether the MMO zone was reached and then held

candidates.name: AntiTemplate
candidates.quote: This trade is a very specific pullback variation that attempts to enter the first pullback after a potential trend change.
candidates.description: The book's named Anti template in full: setup (trend-termination precondition G06-33, then a stronger-than-usual countertrend spike G06-34) + trigger (standard pullback trigger G06-35, or the loose anywhere-in-pullback entry G06-36) + stop (beyond the trend extreme, G06-37) + targets (MMO of the first thrust G06-38, with profit protection if it holds, G06-39).

complexity.reason: aggregates several hard swing-based setup conditions

notes: Trade type: trend termination. Named for Linda Raschke's 'Anti' (Street Smarts, 1996); see G06-62 for her original stochastic-divergence definition, recorded separately since Grimes himself prefers the pure price-structure form given here.

candidates.name: LevelTestedMultipleCleanTimes
candidates.quote: there are levels that have been tested cleanly multiple times, and it is obvious to even a casual chart reader that price has been unable to penetrate the level.
candidates.description: A resistance (support) level -- the highest high (lowest low) of a longer window -- has been approached within a tolerance at least minTests times without closing beyond it, over the window.
candidates.pseudocode: count(i = 1..windowBars, high[i] within touchTolerance * atr(atrLookback) of highest(high, windowBars) AND close[i] <= highest(high, windowBars)) >= minTests

complexity.reason: a touch counter against a window extreme

candidates.name: BreakoutBaseTightRangeNearResistance
candidates.quote: One common form of this pattern is a tight range near the top of a larger range... This small range near a resistance level, usually inside of a larger range, is referred to as a breakout base.
candidates.description: A short recent window's height is small relative to a longer window's height, and sits near the top (long) / bottom (short) of that longer window -- the named 'breakout base'.
candidates.pseudocode: tightHigh = highest(high, tightLookback); tightLow = lowest(low, tightLookback); rangeHigh = highest(high, rangeLookback); rangeLow = lowest(low, rangeLookback); (tightHigh - tightLow) < tightFraction * (rangeHigh - rangeLow) AND (rangeHigh - tightHigh) < proximityFraction * (rangeHigh - rangeLow)

complexity.reason: two window highest/lowest comparisons, no pivots

notes: Same mechanics as Chapter 5's TightRangeNearLargerRangeExtreme and G06-08; the book names this specific instance 'breakout base'.

candidates.name: HigherLowsIntoResistanceBase
candidates.quote: Another variation of this same idea has a market holding successively higher highs into the resistance level... buyers have been willing to buy the market at higher prices on each decline.
candidates.description: An alternate breakout-base form: successive pullback lows into resistance are each higher than the last, without a tight flat base.
candidates.pseudocode: swingLow[0] > swingLow[1] > swingLow[2]

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and multi-leg comparison

candidates.name: PriorPenetrationsWeakenBreakout
candidates.quote: penetrations of levels before the breakout usually seem to expend some of the energy behind the breakout, and often lead to poor trades.
candidates.description: No significant excursion beyond the breakout level occurred in the lookback window before the breakout bar (small failure-test-style probes are fine; a sustained penetration is not).
candidates.pseudocode: NOT (any bar in the last preLookback bars closed beyond level by more than a small tolerance for more than maxPriorBarsBeyond consecutive bars)

complexity.reason: a bounded persistent counter over a lookback window

candidates.name: BidNearBottomOfBaseEntry
candidates.quote: Once the base establishes itself, bid near the bottom of the smaller range.
candidates.description: Breakout-base entry trigger 1: enter (limit) near the low of the base's own recent range.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] <= lowest(low[1], baseLookback) + touchTolerance * atr(atrLookback)
candidates.book_order_type: limit entry near the base low -> mechanized as close-and-next-open once the bar touches the level

complexity.reason: same mechanics as G06-04

candidates.name: SpringEntryInBase
candidates.quote: wait for springs (i.e., drops below the support at the bottom of the base that immediately recover back above the support level) and enter on the close of those bars.
candidates.description: Breakout-base entry trigger 2: enter on the close of a spring (G06-05) at the bottom of the base.
candidates.pseudocode: SpringUpthrustAtRangeExtreme, with rangeLookback set to the base's own lookback
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close of the spring bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: reuses the spring primitive

notes: Not every base features a spring or upthrust, per the book.

candidates.name: EnterAnywhereInBaseSimplified
candidates.quote: Just get the position on, anywhere in the range.
candidates.description: Breakout-base entry trigger 3: once the base (G06-42) has established itself, enter at the next bar's open without waiting for a bottom-of-base or spring trigger.
candidates.pseudocode: BreakoutBaseTightRangeNearResistance -> enter at next open
candidates.book_order_type: market entry at the next bar's open

complexity.reason: a direct entry once the base condition is true

candidates.name: BaseStopBelowLowestPointInBase
candidates.quote: One simple strategy might be to put a stop below the lowest point reached while the market was in the base, with the plan that if you are stopped out on a temporary drop you probably must reenter the trade.
candidates.description: Simple base-entry stop: placed just beyond the lowest low (highest high) reached while the position was accumulating in the base, from entry to the current bar.
candidates.pseudocode: stopPrice = lowest(low, ctx.BarsSinceEntry() + baseLookback) - stopBuffer * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: window low tracked from before entry through the held bars

candidates.name: BaseStopWiderRiskBased
candidates.quote: once the market consolidated below that support level... the probabilities began to favor a breakdown and another trend leg down, so there was no sense in riding the trade to the initial stop level.
candidates.description: A wider, earlier stop for base entries: exit if price consolidates below (above) the base's own support (resistance) for consolidateBars bars, rather than waiting for the initial (looser) stop.
candidates.pseudocode: count(i = 0..consolidateBars-1, close[i] < baseSupportLevel) >= consolidateBars
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (management exit, ahead of the hard stop)

complexity.reason: a persistent counter of consecutive closes beyond a level

candidates.name: BreakoutBaseMmoTarget
candidates.quote: Some traders will set ratio-based targets for breakout trades. Common examples use, for instance, measured move objectives based on the width of the preceding range or the base.
candidates.description: Apply the measured-move-objective mechanics (G06-02) to a breakout-base entry: the width of the base (or the larger preceding range) projected forward from the breakout point.
candidates.pseudocode: target = breakoutLevel + (baseHighPrice - baseLowPrice)

complexity.reason: the base width is already available from G06-42's window extremes, no separate pivot detection needed

notes: Grimes notes prebreakout conditions often feature abnormally contracted volatility, so ratio-based targets from the base width alone can be unnecessarily conservative; he generally prefers no fixed target once the trend is confirmed (see G06-56's notes).

candidates.name: BreakoutEnterInBaseTemplate
candidates.quote: We will first look at some characteristic patterns preceding good breakouts in which the market tips its hand and shows that energy is being built up to support the breakout.
candidates.description: The book's named Breakouts, Entering in the Preceding Base template: setup (level tested multiple clean times G06-41, tight base near resistance G06-42 or higher-lows-into-resistance G06-43, no significant prior penetration G06-44) + trigger (bid near base bottom G06-45, spring entry G06-46, or enter-anywhere G06-47) + stop (initial G06-48, tightened on consolidation G06-49) + target (base-width MMO, G06-50).
candidates.book_order_type: mixed: G06-45 and G06-46 are limit/stop entries, G06-47 is a market entry

complexity.reason: aggregates hard leg/level-counting setup conditions

notes: Trade type: support/resistance breaking (anticipatory entry). This is functionally a support-holding trade taken before the actual breakout.

candidates.name: BreakoutConfirmedByActivityBeyondLevel
candidates.quote: The market has made a successful breakout of an important level. Furthermore, there is good activity (volume, volatility, and price action) beyond the level, proving that it was a valid breakout.
candidates.description: Setup for the Breakout, First Pullback Following template: the breakout bar shows above-average range and above-average volume (reuses Chapter 5's breakout-quality mechanics).
candidates.pseudocode: (high[0] - low[0]) > rangeMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback]) AND volume[0] > volMultiple * average(volume, lookback)

complexity.reason: two window averages

candidates.name: FirstPullbackAfterBreakoutTrigger
candidates.quote: This pullback can be treated as a standard pullback, with any of the standard pullback trigger entries.
candidates.description: After a confirmed breakout (G06-52), enter the resulting pullback with either standard pullback trigger (trend-line failure reversal G06-03, or support/resistance bounce G06-04).
candidates.pseudocode: G06-52 fired earlier AND (G06-03 OR G06-04) on the pullback following it
candidates.book_order_type: mixed: G06-03 is stop/market on the close-back bar, G06-04 is a limit entry

complexity.reason: the same pullback triggers applied after a confirmed breakout

candidates.name: AvoidHoldingPullbackBelowPrebreakoutPivotLow
candidates.quote: It is very hard to justify holding a simple breakout pullback that drops below the pivot low of the prebreakout base, as this type of action is much more indicative of a failed breakout.
candidates.description: Exit the breakout-pullback trade if price trades below (above) the low (high) of the prebreakout base -- a distinguishing invalidation level beyond the standard pullback stop.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < prebreakoutBaseLow
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (management exit, ahead of or in addition to the standard pullback stop)

complexity.reason: needs the prebreakout base's own low carried as position state from before entry

candidates.name: BreakoutFirstPullbackTemplate
candidates.quote: In some sense, this is a hybrid trade, combining characteristics of both breakout and pullback trades, but it can be simplified further: it is really nothing more than a simple pullback trade.
candidates.description: The book's named Breakouts, Entering on First Pullback Following template: setup (confirmed breakout, G06-52) + trigger (standard pullback trigger applied post-breakout, G06-53) + stop (standard pullback stop, plus the prebreakout-pivot invalidation G06-54) + standard pullback targets (G06-18, G06-19, G06-02).
candidates.pseudocode: G06-52 AND G06-53, managed by G06-17 (same as the plain Pullback template) and G06-54, targeting G06-18/G06-19/G06-02

complexity.reason: a thin wrapper around the plain pullback template with one extra invalidation level

notes: Trade type: support/resistance breaking. Trends from good breakout levels tend to run longer, so the book suggests holding more of the position for extension rather than taking full profits at the first target.

candidates.name: BreakoutWeakMomentumSetup
candidates.quote: Good breakouts should have strong momentum, volume, and interest beyond the level. If this does not happen, it is more likely that the breakout will fail.
candidates.description: Warning flag for the Failed Breakouts template: the breakout bar does NOT show above-average range/volume (negation of G06-52) -- raises the odds of failure.
candidates.pseudocode: NOT ((high[0] - low[0]) > rangeMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback]) AND volume[0] > volMultiple * average(volume, lookback))

complexity.reason: negation of G06-52's two window averages

candidates.name: StrongFirstReactionSignalsBreakoutFailure
candidates.quote: If the first reaction is very strong (i.e., the first downswing after an upside breakout or vice versa for a breakdown through support), it suggests a failure of the break interest and greatly increased probability of trade failure.
candidates.description: The first pullback reaction after a breakout moves with strong momentum against the breakout direction (large body relative to recent average range) -- the trigger for treating the breakout as failing.
candidates.pseudocode: close[0] < close[1] AND (open[0] - close[0]) > bodyMultiple * average(high[1..lookback] - low[1..lookback])
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context/entry trigger, may be entered on the close of this bar -> close-and-next-open)

complexity.reason: single-bar body vs. window-average range

notes: This is the same core mechanic as Chapter 5's SharpCountertrendBreaksBreakoutPullback (point C in Figure 5.8), redefined here for the Failed Breakouts template.

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutStopBeyondPullbackThrustExtreme
candidates.quote: the ultimate stop is above the extreme of the initial pullback thrust, but in this trade you must respect your stop fully and without question.
candidates.description: Stop placed just beyond the extreme reached by the initial pullback/reaction thrust after the breakout.
candidates.pseudocode: stopPrice = highest(high, ctx.BarsSinceEntry()) + stopBuffer * ctx.MinMove()

complexity.reason: needs the thrust's own high-water mark since entry

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutTarget
candidates.quote: I tend to be aggressive in taking those profits on failed breakout trades, perhaps even exiting more than half of my position at the first target.
candidates.description: Take a larger-than-usual partial profit (more than half the position) once open profit reaches the initial risk on the trade -- the same mechanics as G06-10, with a larger exitFraction noted.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.OpenPositionProfit() >= riskMultiple * abs(ctx.EntryPrice() - initialStopPrice)

complexity.reason: needs the initial stop distance carried as position state

notes: The exact exit fraction ("more than half") is a position-sizing detail, not itself a bar-level condition; only the trigger price is mechanized here.

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutTemplate
candidates.quote: Most breakouts fail... In terms of actual execution, the breakout failure is nothing more than a failed pullback.
candidates.description: The book's named Failed Breakouts template: setup (weak-momentum breakout, G06-56) + trigger (strong countertrend first reaction, G06-57) + stop (beyond the pullback thrust extreme, G06-58) + target (aggressive initial-risk partial profit, G06-59). May also resolve via a plain failure test at the prior high/low (G06-01), per the book's Goldman Sachs example.
candidates.pseudocode: G06-56 (weak breakout) AND G06-57 (strong countertrend reaction), OR G06-01 applied at the pullback's own extreme; managed by G06-58/G06-59
candidates.book_order_type: market/stop entry on the close of the reaction bar -> close-and-next-open

complexity.reason: aggregates simple/moderate primitives; less pivot-dependent than the other named templates

notes: Trade type: support/resistance holding. The book calls this 'the most complex and least well defined of the major trade setups' despite its comparatively simple mechanics, because judging trigger timing in real time is hard.

candidates.name: RaschkeAntiStochasticDivergence
candidates.quote: she gives a specific definition of this trade in that it quantifies the momentums on two time frames using the stochastic indicator. The pattern essentially is that the fast and slow lines of the indicator are sloping against each other.
candidates.description: Linda Raschke's original 'Anti' confirmation (cited by Grimes, who prefers pure price structure instead): a fast (shorter-lookback) stochastic is rising while a slow (longer-lookback) stochastic is falling, or vice versa -- two time frames' momentum sloping against each other.
candidates.pseudocode: stochastic(fastLookback)[0] > stochastic(fastLookback)[1] AND stochastic(slowLookback)[0] < stochastic(slowLookback)[1]
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (alternate confirmation filter, not required by Grimes's own method)

complexity.reason: two stochastic oscillators plus a slope comparison

notes: Cited from Linda Raschke, Street Smarts (1996); Grimes explicitly says his own preference is the price-structure form (G06-33/G06-34/G06-35), not this indicator definition, so this candidate is not included in the AntiTemplate composite.

rejected.quote: My preference is to put stops farther away from the pattern, and to introduce a small random 'jitter' element to stop placement.
rejected.reason: explicitly introduces randomness into stop placement, which the mining brief excludes; the deterministic buffer portion of the same statement is captured as G06-17

rejected.quote: Assume you want to risk $10,000 on each trade, and you just booked a $10,000 loss on a simple pullback, which, a few days later, is clearly developing into a complex pullback. What now?

rejected.quote: Trader A indiscriminately buys in the base and manages the trades... Trader B is much more precise with his entries and always bids at the bottom of the range.

rejected.quote: This is a reliable pattern on all time frames, and is especially powerful for intraday traders when combined with time-of-day influences.
rejected.reason: no concrete time-of-day condition is given, too vague to mechanize even with a default parameter

rejected.quote: Many traders will be tempted to skip these trades, as they will be forced to enter at significantly higher prices than they had planned, and will be exposed to the danger of a gap failure.

rejected.quote: It is well known by now that the core entry technique of the system the Turtles were taught was a breakout of a 20-day or 55-day channel.

chapter_summary: The book's core practical chapter: eight named trade templates built from three primary trades (failure test, pullback, breakout) plus five derived combinations (the Anti, complex pullbacks, lower-time-frame-breakout pullback, breakout-entered-in-base, breakout-entered-on-first-pullback, failed breakouts). Every template is mined as setup/trigger/stop/target/invalidation atoms plus one composite candidate per template (G06-13, G06-21, G06-26, G06-32, G06-40, G06-51, G06-55, G06-60) listing its parts via composes. Shared primitives (failure-test trigger G06-01, measured-move target G06-02, trend-line/channel failure entry G06-03, support/resistance bounce entry G06-04, spring/upthrust G06-05, climax bar G06-06) are defined once at the top of this file and reused across templates via composes/depends_on. Complex, ABCD, and change-of-character setup conditions are honestly graded hard/research since they need swing-pivot detection; the failure test and failed-breakout templates are the most mechanizable (moderate throughout). Chapter 5 defines equivalent primitives independently under its own G05 IDs per the mining convention; the dedup pass should merge the two sets.
